questions_asked:
# Expert Question 1 (round 1/10)

When field investigators get a hornet report from a citizen, do they usually rely on the
citizen's own photo to decide whether to send an investigator, or do they use the
reporter's words (insect name mentioned, size, behavior) and location instead? Which of
the two matters most to them in practice?

# Expert Question 2 (round 2/10)

Builds on your first answer (location is the strongest triage filter). How close does a
citizen's sighting need to be to a confirmed giant-hornet finding before your
investigators really take it seriously?

# Expert Question 3 (round 3/10)

Builds on the 5 km / 20–30 km tiers. If a report turns out to be another insect, how long
after the state tells the reporter the result does the reporter usually stay away from
reporting the same thing again?

# Expert Question 4 (round 4/10)

You said location near a confirmed finding is the strongest triage filter. If two reports
are equally close to a known finding, but one is from a small town and the other from a
big city, do your investigators treat them the same, or does the area change how hard
they work the report?

# Expert Question 5 (round 5/10)

Your triage relies heavily on the reporter's own words in the note. If the note is very
short, or full of typos, or says nothing about size or behavior, how much do
investigators trust that note, compared with a detailed, clear one?

# Expert Question 6 (round 6/10)

Reports come in by phone, email, and a web form, and sometimes the same person or the
same insect gets reported twice from nearby. In practice, do you treat a second
nearby report from a different person as more credible than a single one, or does a
repeat from the same person count against it?

# Expert Question 7 (round 7/10)

The hornet queens wake up in spring and new colonies appear over the warm months. When a
new confirmed nest is found in a place the pest was not known to be, do investigators
expect more sightings to keep coming from that same area, or is a single isolated
sighting usually just that — a one-off?

# Expert Question 8 (round 8/10)

The state has limited staff and budget, so it cannot follow up on every report. In a
busy season, roughly how many new sightings can the investigation team realistically
go out and look into, in a given month?

# Expert Question 9 (round 9/10)

To call the giant hornet eradicated from a state, how long would it need to go with no
new confirmed nest, and would you still keep checking certain places even after that
quiet period?

# Expert Question 10 (round 10/10)

As new reports and lab results keep coming in throughout the season, how often does
your triage or prioritization get refreshed — daily, weekly, monthly — and is there any
trigger that makes you refresh it right away, even off-schedule?
expert_answers:
In practice, the reporter's words and location matter most for triage; the photo is secondary and often unusable.

Reasons: a large share of citizen photos are blurry, distant, poorly lit, or show no insect at all, so they cannot support a confident ID. Triage is done fast by phone/email screeners who are not entomologists, and they work from the text fields (insect name given, described size, behavior, whether it was attacking bees, whether it was near a known detection) plus geography and date. Location is the strongest single filter, because confirmed detections are highly clustered and a report near a prior positive gets priority regardless of photo quality.

Photos become decisive mainly when they are clear enough for an expert to confirm or exclude, which is a minority of submissions. So: text plus location for prioritization, photo for confirmation when it is good.

Within roughly 5 km of a confirmed detection, a report is taken seriously almost regardless of other features; that is the radius where investigators will typically follow up.

Beyond that, the practical tiers are: out to about 20–30 km (the queen's dispersal range) a report is still treated as plausible and gets screened carefully, but only prioritized if the text is strong (attacking bees, correct size/description, good photo). Past ~30 km from any confirmed finding, a report is generally treated as a low-priority outlier unless it is a clear photo or comes with a second independent report nearby.

These are empirical operational judgments, not hard thresholds — the exact cutoff varies with how many reports are pending and how many positives have already been found.

Mostly they don't come back at all. Once a reporter is told "that was a paper wasp / yellowjacket, not the Asian giant hornet," the large majority never submit another report — there is no meaningful "cooldown" period because they simply stop.

Among the minority who do report again, the gap is typically on the order of a season to a year, not days or weeks: they report again only when they see something new the following spring/summer, and usually only if the new sighting looks different to them. Repeat reports within days of a negative determination are uncommon and are usually a different household member or a genuinely new insect.

So for modeling purposes: a negative result acts as a near-permanent suppression on that reporter, with re-reporting, when it happens, clustered at roughly annual intervals. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured rate.

They are not treated the same. A report from a small town or rural area is worked harder than an equally close report from a big city.

Reasons: in a dense urban setting, a single report is more likely to be a misidentification (many people, many insects, many reports, most negative), and a lone hornet there is less likely to indicate an established colony. In a small town or rural area near a confirmed finding, the same report carries more weight because there are fewer observers, so a report represents a larger fraction of the local observation effort, and the surrounding habitat (woodlots, apiaries, open ground for overwintering queens) is more suitable for a nest.

So the practical effect is that the effective priority radius is wider in rural/small-town settings and narrower in dense urban ones, even at equal distance from a confirmed detection.

A short or sloppy note is trusted much less, but it is not discarded — it is downgraded, not ignored.

In practice: a detailed note that names the insect, gives size, describes behavior (attacking bees, hovering, nest location), and matches the season is treated as strong evidence and can push a report up a tier on its own. A one-line note ("saw a big hornet") or one full of typos and no size/behavior information carries little weight; screeners treat it as weak and fall back on the other signals — location relative to confirmed findings, date, and whether a usable photo exists.

The key point is that a weak note does not lower the report's priority below what location alone would give it. A vague note near a confirmed detection still gets followed up; a vague note far from any detection stays low priority. A detailed note can raise a distant report; a vague note cannot.

So the note acts as an upward modifier when it is rich, and as a near-neutral factor when it is poor — it rarely pushes a report down on its own.

A second nearby report from a different person is treated as more credible — it is one of the strongest corroborating signals available, and it can raise a report a tier on its own, especially when the two reports are close in space and time and describe the same thing.

A repeat from the same person counts against it, mildly. It is treated as one report, not two: the duplicate is collapsed, and if the person has already been told a prior report was negative, the new one is discounted further (consistent with the near-permanent suppression effect). Same-person repeats add no independent evidence.

So: independent reporters near each other = corroboration, up-weighted; same reporter repeating = deduplicated and slightly discounted.

A new confirmed nest is not a one-off — it reliably generates a cluster of further reports from the same area, and investigators expect that.

Reasons: a nest means many workers foraging over the season within a few km, so multiple residents see them; the public announcement of a confirmed finding also triggers a burst of reports from that neighborhood (awareness effect). So a confirmed nest typically produces a local cluster of reports over the following weeks to months, concentrated within roughly the queen's dispersal/foraging radius (a few km, extending to ~20–30 km for new queens).

A single isolated sighting far from any confirmed nest, with no follow-up reports, is usually treated as a probable one-off misidentification — unless it is a clear photo or is corroborated by an independent nearby report.

Caveat: the cluster is expected but not guaranteed; a nest found late in the season may yield few additional reports before the colony dies off.

In a busy season, a state invasive-species team like Washington's can realistically do on the order of a few dozen field follow-ups per month — call it roughly 20–50 investigations/month, with the higher end only if the team is fully staffed and reports are clustered so one trip covers several.

The binding constraint is field time, not screening: each follow-up is typically a half-day to a full day per site (travel, search, sometimes trap placement), and the team is small — a handful of field staff, not dozens. So the practical throughput is a few per working day at most, and often less once travel distances across the state are counted.

This is an empirical operational estimate, not a measured figure; the exact number scales with staffing and how tightly reports cluster geographically.

For a pest like this, "eradicated" is normally declared only after **three consecutive years** with no confirmed nest, no confirmed specimen, and no credible photo-verified sighting — i.e., three full life cycles with no evidence of a reproducing population. Two years is sometimes argued, but three is the standard cautious bar because a small colony can go undetected for a season, and overwintering queens can produce a nest the following year.

Yes, you keep checking after the quiet period. Surveillance is not stopped at declaration: you maintain traps and sentinel apiaries, and you keep focusing on the historically high-risk places — around prior confirmed nests, the original Vancouver Island/Whatcom County area, ports and border crossings (where new introductions arrive), and apiaries. That targeted monitoring continues for several years past the declaration, because the realistic failure mode is a fresh reintroduction, not survival of the old population.

These are empirical/regulatory judgments, not measured thresholds.
